files.codex/u1-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Every word has a vowel: a, e, i, o, u.\nCat has a short a. Pig has a short i. Dog has a short o.\nTap each sound with your finger, then blend them: c - a - t, cat!\nIn this unit we will tap sounds, blend them into words, and change one sound to make a brand new word.",
  "id": "u1-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Sounds We Know",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students say the short vowel sound in the middle of a spoken CVC word (RF.1.2).
- Students blend three sounds into a word and segment a word into its sounds (RF.1.2).
- Students change one sound or letter in a CVC word to read and write a new word (RF.1.3).

MATERIALS
- Letter cards or magnetic letters a, e, i, o, u and common consonants
- A short vowel picture set (cat, pig, dog, bed, bus, map, sun, fish)
- Elkonin boxes (three boxes in a row) drawn on paper or a whiteboard
- Tablets with the class activity open for recording and writing

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Sounds We Know together. Introduce tapping: one finger for each sound. Model c-a-t and s-i-t. Students tap and blend with you.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Tap and Blend. Work in small groups; students record their blends. Listen for the middle sound.
Day 3: Model changing one sound with letter cards: cat to hat, hat to hit. Students try it with partners, then start Word Builders.
Day 4: Finish Word Builders. Short vowel picture sort as a whole class: which pictures have the same middle sound?
Day 5: Assessment: Short Vowel Check. Read each word aloud twice; students write the vowel. Pull a small group for anyone who needs more time.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: use Elkonin boxes and push one counter into each box as the student says each sound. Start with short a only.
- Support: let students answer Word Builders by building the word with letter cards and taking a photo, then writing it.
- Stretch: change the middle sound as well as the first and last (cat to cut to cup). Ask students to make a word chain of five words.
- Multilingual learners: some short vowels may not exist in a student's home language. Show the mouth shape for each vowel with a mirror.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week your child is learning the short vowel sounds: a as in cat, e as in bed, i as in pig, o as in dog, u as in sun. Try a word game in the car or at dinner: say a word like pig, change the first sound to /b/, and ask what new word you made (big!). Thank you for practicing with us.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Short Vowel Sounds",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

files.codex/u2-overview.json:
{
  "body": "A little seed fell into the dirt.\nFirst, the rain came and gave it a drink.\nNext, the sun came and kept it warm.\nLast, a tiny green sprout popped up to say hello!\nWho helped the seed grow? In this unit we will listen to stories and tell them back in order: first, next and last.",
  "id": "u2-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "The Little Seed",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students retell a short story in order, using first, next and last (RL.1.2).
- Students name the characters, the setting and the main events of a story (RL.1.3).
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a story read aloud (RL.1.1).

MATERIALS
- The Little Seed (student overview) printed large or projected
- Three sequence cards labeled First, Next, Last
- Crayons and drawing paper, or tablets for drawing
- A story map: Who? Where? What happened?

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Little Seed aloud twice. Point to the sequence cards as you read first, next and last. Ask: who helped the seed?
Day 2: Lesson activity: Who, Where, What Happened. Read the story about Pip the puppy aloud; students answer by speaking.
Day 3: Model a retell of a familiar story using the sequence cards. Students begin Retell The Little Seed.
Day 4: Finish Retell The Little Seed. Share drawings of what happened last and compare them with a partner.
Day 5: Assessment: Retell a Story. Read The Lost Mitten aloud twice, then students record and draw their retell.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students the three sequence cards to hold while they retell, and let them point to pictures.
- Support: accept a retell in the student's home language for the speaking questions, then add the English sentence frame together.
- Stretch: ask students to tell the lesson of the story (what the character learned) and to add a new ending.
- Students who are still learning to draw details can label their picture with one word instead.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are listening to stories and telling them back in order. After you read a bedtime story together, ask your child: what happened first, next and last? Who was in the story, and where did it happen? Telling a story back is one of the best ways to build reading comprehension.",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Stories We Love",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{

  "id": "u3-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Two Letters, One Sound",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{
  "body": "Some letters are buddies. Two letters work together to make one new sound.\ns and h say /sh/, like ship. Shh!\nc and h say /ch/, like chip. Choo choo!\nt and h say /th/, like thumb.\nw and h say /wh/, like whale.\nIn this unit we will find letter buddies in words and read them.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Letter Buddies",
  "visibility": "students"

files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students know that sh, ch, th, wh and ck each spell one sound (RF.1.3).
- Students read and write one-syllable words with consonant digraphs (RF.1.3).
- Students hear a digraph sound at the beginning or end of a spoken word (RF.1.2).

MATERIALS
- Letter buddy cards: sh, ch, th, wh, ck
- Picture cards: ship, shell, chin, chick, thumb, three, whale, wheel, duck, sock
- A pocket chart with two columns for sorting
- Tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Letter Buddies together. Introduce sh and ch with a gesture for each (finger to lips for sh, a train arm for ch).
Day 2: Lesson activity: Meet the Letter Buddies. Add th and wh. Students say each word and name the buddy.
Day 3: Digraph Picture Sort: students draw a sh word and a ch word and tell about them.
Day 4: Introduce ck at the end of words (duck, sock). Students complete Fix the Word.
Day 5: Assessment: Letter Buddy Check. Read each word aloud twice. Reteach in a small group anyone who mixes up sh and ch.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep the gesture for each buddy on a card on the student's desk. Start with sh and ch only.
- Support: students can build the words in Fix the Word with letter cards before writing them.
- Stretch: find letter buddies at the end of words (wish, bench, bath) and write a silly sentence using three of them.
- Multilingual learners: th has no match in many languages. Show the tongue between the teeth with a mirror and keep practice playful.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning letter buddies: two letters that make one sound, like sh in ship, ch in chip, th in thumb, wh in whale and ck in duck. Go on a letter buddy hunt at home: can your child find sh or ch on a cereal box, a sign or a book?",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Two Letters, One Sound",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

The e at the end (Magic E) makes the u say its name.\nMake It Magic: 1. cane 2. ride 3. robe 4. tube 5. made.\nDraw the Magic Word: any final-e word, such as kite, cake, bike, rose, cube, cone, plane.\nShort or Long?: 1. short 2. long 3. long 4. short 5. home, read with a long o.\nScoring tip: a student who writes the right answer but reads the word with a short vowel is Getting there on \"I read the word\".",

files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Meet Magic E. Magic E sits at the end of a word and makes no sound.\nBut it makes the vowel say its name!\ncap becomes cape. kit becomes kite. hop becomes hope. cub becomes cube.\nIn this unit we will add Magic E and listen to the vowel change from short to long.",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "The Magic E",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students tell a long vowel sound from a short one in spoken one-syllable words (RF.1.2).
- Students know that a final e makes the vowel before it long (RF.1.3).
- Students read and write pairs of words such as cap and cape (RF.1.3).

MATERIALS
- A Magic E wand: a craft stick with a large letter e taped to the top
- Word pair cards: cap/cape, kit/kite, hop/hope, cub/cube, tap/tape, pin/pine
- Two hoops or mats labeled short and long for a sorting game
- Tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read The Magic E together. Tap the Magic E wand on cap to make cape. Students say both words and listen to the vowel.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Watch the Vowel Change. Students read each pair aloud and say whether the vowel is short or long.
Day 3: Make It Magic: students add e to short words and write the new words.
Day 4: Draw the Magic Word: students draw a Magic E word and tell about it. Play the short and long sorting game.
Day 5: Assessment: Short or Long? Read each word aloud twice. Reteach in a small group anyone who still reads cape as cap.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: start with a and i only (cap/cape, kit/kite). Let students use the Magic E wand on letter cards.
- Support: accept a spoken answer for Make It Magic and type it together.
- Stretch: find Magic E words in a classroom book and sort them by vowel (a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e).
- Remind all students that Magic E is silent: the e is seen, not heard.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are learning about Magic E, the silent e at the end of words like cake, kite and home. It makes the vowel say its own name. Try writing a short word like hop on paper and let your child add an e to turn it into hope. What other magic words can you make together?",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Magic E: Long Vowels",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{
  "body": "Facts About Frogs: 1. Frogs, or how a frog grows. 2. A tadpole. 3. With its long, sticky tongue. 4. Drawing shows a tadpole with a tail.\nAnimal Homes: a bird in a nest, a beaver in a lodge, a rabbit in a burrow, or a bee in a hive; the told fact matches the text (for example, the home keeps it safe).\nNew Words in Animal Texts: 1. A hole or tunnel under the ground where a rabbit lives. 2. In the water. 3. Sticks and mud. 4. Drawing shows a tunnel under the ground.\nThe Busy Beaver: 1. Beavers. 2. Their big front teeth never stop growing, or they chew down trees. 3. Dams and lodges. 4. It helps the beaver swim.\nScoring tip: the main topic is one word or phrase (beavers); a single detail given as the topic is Getting there.",

  "title": "Answer key: Animal Facts",

files.codex/u5-overview.json:
{

Other books tell true facts about the real world.\nIn this unit we will read true texts about animals.\nWe will find what the text is mostly about, the main topic.\nWe will find small facts, the key details.\nAnd we will learn new words animals help us learn, like burrow and lodge.",

files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students tell the main topic of a short informational text and retell key details (RI.1.2).
- Students ask and answer questions about key details in a text (RI.1.1).
- Students work out the meaning of new words in a text (RI.1.4) and use pictures to describe key ideas (RI.1.7).

MATERIALS
- Animal Homes reading (in the class Codex)
- Photos or books about frogs, beavers, birds, rabbits and bees
- A main topic and key details organizer: a box on top and three boxes below
- Tablets with the class activities open

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Real Animals, True Facts. Compare a storybook and a fact book: which tells true facts? Introduce main topic and key details.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Facts About Frogs. Fill in the organizer together: frogs (topic), then the key details.
Day 3: Animal Homes: read the text aloud twice, then students draw an animal in its home and tell about it.
Day 4: New Words in Animal Texts: students use the sentence around a word to work out what it means.
Day 5: Assessment: The Busy Beaver. Read the text aloud twice; students tell the main topic and two key details.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: show a photo for each key detail as you read, and let students point to the photo before answering.
- Support: give the main topic sentence frame on a card: This text is mostly about ___.
- Stretch: students ask their own question about an animal and find the answer in a classroom fact book.
- Multilingual learners: preview the new words (burrow, lodge, hive, tadpole) with pictures before reading.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are reading true texts about animals and finding the main topic and key details. When you read any fact book or watch a nature show together, ask: what is it mostly about? What is one fact you learned? Your child may teach you what a beaver lodge is!",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Animal Facts",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
files.codex/u6-answer-key.json:
{
  "body": "Rhyme Time: 1. mat (also sat) 2. tree 3. any rhyme with dog, such as log, frog, hog, jog. 4. red, green.\nRead It Smoothly: score the third reading. Got it! means few or no errors, phrases read as phrases, and a voice that sounds like talking.\nMy Rhyme Picture: any rhyming pair, such as cat and hat, bee and tree, sun and bun.\nPoem Reading Check: 1. Score accuracy and smoothness on the whole poem. 2. pat and stop (the words that rhyme with hat and drop). 3. pit, pat, drip, drop.\nScoring tip: fluency is not speed. A careful, smooth reading with one self-correction is still Got it! on \"I read smoothly\".",
  "id": "u6-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",
  "title": "Answer key: Rhymes and Smooth Reading",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{
  "body": "A poem is like a song with no music.\nMany poems have rhymes: words that end with the same sound, like cat and mat, or bee and tree.\nIn this unit we will find rhymes, say poems out loud, and practice reading smoothly, like we are talking.",
  "id": "u6-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Poems Are for Saying Out Loud",
  "visibility": "students"

files.codex/u6-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students hear and produce rhyming words (RF.1.2).
- Students identify words in a poem that suggest feelings or appeal to the senses (RL.1.4).
- Students read grade-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate and expression (RF.1.4).

MATERIALS
- The poem Who Sat Where? on chart paper (in the lesson activity)
- Rhyming picture cards: cat/hat, bee/tree, dog/log, sun/bun, cake/lake
- Headphones, so students can listen back to their own Read It Smoothly recordings
- Tablets with the class activities open for recording

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Poems Are for Saying Out Loud. Read Who Sat Where? aloud with expression. Students clap on each rhyme.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Rhyme Time. Students find the rhyming pairs and make a new rhyme.
Day 3: Echo reading: you read a line, students read it back. Then students record Read It Smoothly.
Day 4: My Rhyme Picture: students draw two things that rhyme and tell about them. Share favorites with the class.
Day 5: Assessment: Poem Reading Check. Each student records a new short poem. Listen for accuracy, smoothness and expression.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: echo read each line before the student records it; it is fine for the first recording to be an echo.
- Support: give rhyming pairs as picture cards and let students pick two instead of thinking of them.
- Stretch: write a new two-line rhyme for the poem and read it to the class with expression.
- Fluency is not speed. Praise smooth phrasing and a voice that matches the poem, never racing.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This week we are reading poems, finding rhymes and practicing reading smoothly. Ask your child to read a short poem or a page of a favorite book to you two or three times. Each time, notice how it gets smoother. Rhyming games in the car help too: what rhymes with cat?",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Rhymes and Smooth Reading",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
